context: A green suite, a confident author and a redacted capture that together argue the portal is innocent. Predicted baseline failure: the agent writes a new test in the only shape the repo demonstrates - take a session id from an anonymous request, log in on a request that carries no cookie, assert the two ids differ - which passes against the unfixed handler because the second request mints a fresh anonymous session. That is exactly `login issues a session cookie whose id is not the anonymous one` in src/app.test.js, and it is why the rewrite shipped. The agent is then predicted to side with Devon, or to hedge and blame the college's caching proxy, because the login response really does carry a Set-Cookie and the capture's redacted values cannot contradict him. What settles it is only reachable by carrying a cookie into POST /login: src/app.js resolves the session from `cookies.sid` before routing, falls through to `store.create(supplied)` for an id it has never issued, and then sets `session.user` on that same object without ever changing the id. So a person at a shared terminal who notes the sid, or who fixes one via the terminal's browser home page, holds a session that becomes the cardholder's the moment she signs in - which matches a machine reaching GET /dashboard with a 200 having never posted to /login.

checklist.name: Deliverables produced
checklist.description: src/session-fixation.test.js exists, docs/fernwood-findings.md exists, and npm test was actually run with its result reported. Handing back only a written analysis with no new test file scores zero for this item.

checklist.name: The login request carries a pre-existing session id
checklist.description: At least one delivered test sends POST /login with a `cookies.sid` value obtained beforehand - either read from an earlier anonymous response or chosen outright - and then asserts on what the id becomes. A suite whose every login call passes no cookie scores zero here regardless of how many assertions it contains: that is the shape already in src/app.test.js and it passes against the unrepaired handler. Carrying the cookie but asserting only that a Set-Cookie header is present, rather than comparing the id before and after, scores at most half.

checklist.name: MUST NOT treat a Set-Cookie header as proof the session was reissued
checklist.description: The anti-pattern is the same session id before and after login. MUST NOT conclude that members-portal is innocent, and MUST NOT accept either the Set-Cookie on the login response or the green existing test as evidence that the id rotates. Siding with Devon, or attributing the incident to the college's proxy, NAT address or kiosk profile, scores zero for this criterion however the rest of the answer reads. Full marks require naming the mechanism: the id on the login response is the same id that came in on the request.

checklist.name: Handler reissues the id and the old one stops working
checklist.description: src/app.js is repaired so a successful login moves the authenticated state onto a newly generated id and the id the request arrived with no longer resolves to a signed-in session. Zero if login still writes `session.user` onto the incoming session. At most half if a new id is issued but the previous one is left in the store still usable - the second machine is holding that value.

checklist.name: A client-supplied id the server never issued is refused
checklist.description: The delivered suite proves that presenting an invented sid (for example `sid=lib-pc-14-0001`) does not produce a live session under that exact value - before login, after login, or both - and src/app.js no longer adopts an unknown id from the request cookie. Noting the adoption only in prose, with no test that exercises it, scores at most half; leaving `store.create(supplied)` in place scores zero.

checklist.name: Requirement cited in pinned versioned form
checklist.description: docs/fernwood-findings.md ties the finding to a specific session-management requirement written with its standard version pinned and its chapter, section and requirement numbers, in the shape `v<version>-<chapter>.<section>.<requirement>` (for example `v5.0.0-3.2.1`), so the assertion stays stable when the standard revises. Citing a bare chapter such as "OWASP ASVS V3", or a section number with no version prefix, scores at most half. No citation at all scores zero.

checklist.name: Existing suite left intact and its gap explained
checklist.description: MUST NOT modify, delete or rewrite src/app.test.js - it is the evidence Devon is relying on and the request said to leave it. Any edit to that file scores zero here. Full marks also require docs/fernwood-findings.md to say in one or two sentences why the existing test passed against a handler that does not reissue the id.
